strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: exploiting information asymmetry (solving forward is easier than planning backward) to construct long-horizon tasks from chained, easily executable subtasks, enabling controllable difficulty levels.

Substantial empirical artifact: a fully automated pipeline producing 6,000+ diverse tasks with trajectories in OSWorld, spanning many software applications and domains, plus demonstrated generality by applying the same pipeline to a web environment (InSTA).

Thorough dataset analysis: human evaluation of 100 samples across quality dimensions, statistics on token counts, step counts, and multi-tool usage, and a detailed, transparent cost analysis ($0.60/trajectory) with explicit assumptions and comparisons to human annotation costs.

Benchmark results are informative: consistent performance degradation from 18% to 4% across difficulty levels, human comparison (~70% on hardest tier), and a useful taxonomy of failure modes (grounding, state tracking, error recovery).
Good reproducibility posture: full prompt templates, action space definition, cost breakdowns, and stated public release of code/data.
weaknesses: Circularity in evaluation: task success is judged by an LLM-based verifier built from the same model family (GPT-4.1) used to generate the tasks and trajectories; despite 89% verifier accuracy, ~11% systematic error in a benchmark whose headline numbers are 2-18% success rates is concerning. No programmatic/scripted verifiers or holdout human re-verification of benchmark results are provided.

Evaluation uses bare LLMs with minimal scaffolding on only 50 tasks per level (20 at level 6 for humans). The paper claims to evaluate 'state-of-the-art' agents, but omitting optimized agent scaffolds (e.g., the computer-use-preview model in its intended agentic loop, or established agent frameworks known to perform substantially better on OSWorld) may substantially underestimate model capability and overstate benchmark difficulty.

Difficulty is operationalized purely as subtask count / horizon length; the paper acknowledges this conflates horizon with intrinsic complexity, but no experiment disentangles them, weakening the 'fine-grained difficulty control' claim.

Positioning as a training resource is untested: no fine-tuning, curriculum learning, or RL experiments demonstrate that the synthetic trajectories actually improve agents, leaving the central practical value claim (beyond benchmarking) speculative.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior synthetic-task pipelines (Explorer, AgentTrek, Synatra, WorkArena++ compositional tasks); the main differentiators are the desktop/pixel-level setting and the two-stage planner-grounder executor, which are engineering contributions more than conceptual ones.

Cost comparison to human-annotated benchmarks ($4-$425/task) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: AgentSynth tasks deliberately exclude login, credentials, and backend-modifying actions, making them cheaper and simpler to verify than the real-work tasks in TheAgentCompany or OSWorld.
Small human evaluation (100 samples) and no inter-annotator agreement statistics; some quality metrics (e.g., 'Verifier Accuracy' at 89%) leave meaningful ambiguity about label noise.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and timely problem: the cost and labor bottleneck of building computer-use agent datasets, and the proposed subtask-chaining pipeline is a sensible, fully automated solution with a detailed cost breakdown ($0.60/trajectory) that is convincingly cheaper than human annotation.
Controllable difficulty via the number of summarized subtasks is a useful and well-motivated design knob, demonstrated with clear examples (Section 4.2) and dataset statistics (Figure 2).

The evaluation is reasonably broad: four frontier models across six difficulty levels, per-domain breakdowns, a small human baseline, and an additional experiment in the InSTA web environment showing generality of the pipeline.

Human quality evaluation of 100 sampled tasks with multiple criteria (feasibility, coherence, persona relevance, verifier accuracy) is a positive practice, and prompt templates in the appendix support reproducibility.
The failure mode analysis (Section 5.3) provides useful qualitative insights into why agents fail on long-horizon GUI tasks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea of chaining solvable subtasks and summarizing them into harder composite tasks is an incremental combination of existing techniques. The paper itself acknowledges close predecessors (Explorer, AgentTrek, InSTA, Synatra), and the main new element — applying the idea to OSWorld with a two-stage planner/grounding executor — is an engineering contribution rather than a conceptual advance.

Circularity in evaluation: the same LLM-based verifier (built on GPT-4.1) is used both to construct the dataset and to judge task success for the benchmarked models. With only ~89% verifier-human agreement reported on a small 100-sample check, and success rates in the 0-18% range, verifier noise could materially distort the reported results. Programmatic or human-verified scoring on a subset of evaluation runs is needed.

Generator-evaluator bias: tasks are proposed, executed, verified, and judged largely by GPT-4.1-family models. This risks systematically encoding the generator's capabilities/biases into the benchmark, yet the paper does not analyze this (e.g., whether models from a different family find GPT-4.1-generated tasks artificially easy or hard).

No training experiment: the abstract and conclusion claim AgentSynth is well-suited for training/curriculum learning, but no fine-tuning or RL results are presented; claims about training value are unsupported.

Weak evaluation protocol details: only 50 tasks per difficulty level (and 20 for the human baseline at level 6), no statistical significance testing, no variance across runs for the main benchmark, and bare-LLM prompting without standard agent scaffolds weakens claims about 'state-of-the-art agents' struggling.

The human evaluation is small (100 instances) and its inter-annotator agreement and annotator counts are not reported; 'Verifier Accuracy' of 89% is presented as a strength but leaves 11% label noise in a benchmark where the discriminative signal being claimed is small.

Difficulty is conflated with horizon: the paper concedes level n is defined only by subtask count, so the headline result 'success drops from 18% to 4%' partially reflects trajectory length and token/context limits rather than intrinsic task complexity.

Presentation issues: several typos (e.g., 'clike', 'hockey' for hotkey), and Table 4's qualitative 'multi-domain/long-horizon' comparison is self-served by the authors' own definitions rather than an empirical comparison.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated contribution: the pipeline addresses a real bottleneck (costly human annotation of computer-use tasks) and delivers a concrete, sizable resource (6,000+ tasks and trajectories) built on OSWorld, a realistic desktop environment.

The core idea of information asymmetry (generate forward, evaluate forward-solvable but backward-hard tasks) is sensible and the multi-agent pipeline (proposer, executor, verifier, reviser, follow-up proposer, summarizer) is well engineered, including graceful handling of partial failures via task revision.

Controllable difficulty via the number of chained subtasks is a genuinely useful property for benchmark design and curriculum-style future use, and the difficulty levels are validated empirically (token counts, step counts, model performance gradients).

Evaluation includes multiple components: human quality assessment across four metrics (~87-94%), cost analysis with transparent assumptions, benchmarking of four frontier models across difficulty levels and domains, a human baseline (~70% on level 6), and a second environment (InSTA) demonstrating generality of the pipeline.

The paper is transparent about limitations (horizon-vs-intrinsic-difficulty confound, exclusion of login tasks, unexplored training use) and releases code, data, and full prompts, supporting reproducibility.
The failure-mode analysis (imprecise clicking, state tracking, error recovery) is informative and consistent with the broader literature, adding qualitative value beyond raw numbers.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Chaining LLM-executed subtasks and summarizing them into harder tasks closely mirrors prior work (Explorer, Synatra, AgentTrek); the main delta is application to OS-level desktop environments and a two-stage planner/grounding executor. The paper acknowledges this but the methodological novelty is modest for a top-tier venue.

The benchmark's headline claim (models collapse from 18% to 4%) rests on a specific, minimal evaluation setup: bare models with a generic pyautogui prompt, no scaffolding, and only 50 tasks per level. The near-zero success at high levels may partly reflect the deliberately weak evaluation harness rather than task impossibility; no optimized or agentic scaffolds (e.g., stronger planners, set-of-marks grounding, retry loops) are tested, making the 'discriminative power' claim harder to interpret.

Task success is judged by an LLM-based verifier (89% human agreement per their own sample), which is both the gatekeeping mechanism for data quality and the grading mechanism at test time. There is a circularity risk, and no programmatic or state-based verification is provided; error bars/confidence intervals around the 89% figure and per-level verifier agreement are not reported.

Tasks within a trajectory are nested (level-n tasks are prefixes of level-n+1), so the 300 benchmark tasks are highly correlated, effectively reducing the independent sample size; the statistical robustness of the reported differences is unclear.
No training experiments: the paper repeatedly claims suitability for training/curriculum RL but provides zero fine-tuning evidence, leaving a central part of the motivation unvalidated.

The difficulty metric conflates horizon length with intrinsic difficulty, as the authors admit; difficulty-level comparisons across models could therefore reflect length-robustness rather than capability in a well-controlled sense.

The cost comparison to human annotation ($0.60 vs $4-$425) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: human-built benchmarks include programmatic success checkers and vetted solvability guarantees, whereas AgentSynth trajectories are self-generated and self-verified; the comparison also depends on arguable assumptions about labor rates and omitted setup costs.
Reliance on live external websites introduces benchmark instability and potential non-reproducibility over time (task state and content may change), which is not discussed.

Human evaluation covers only 100 instances with no inter-annotator agreement statistics, and the safety/scope restrictions (no login, no email/social) exclude a large fraction of realistic productivity tasks, acknowledged but limiting real-world coverage.

strengths: The core idea—exploiting information asymmetry between trajectory generation and evaluation to synthesize hard long-horizon tasks from reliably-solvable subtasks—is clean, well-motivated, and clearly differentiates the paper from retroactive task-labeling approaches like OS-Genesis and Learn-by-interact.

The validation is unusually thorough for a data-generation paper: human quality assessment across four metrics, verifier calibration against human judgment (including a graded partial-credit signal), an adversarial near-miss/benign perturbation stress test, and an information-asymmetry ablation (Table 5) that convincingly isolates the pipeline's contribution (generation success 64%→11% for direct instruction vs. stable ~52-65% for AgentSynth, while evaluation success diverges as intended).

Difficulty is controllable along multiple correlated axes (horizon, memory span, app count, app switches, Table C.1), which is a meaningful methodological advantage over benchmarks with fixed difficulty.
Generality is demonstrated beyond the main environment via the InSTA web-agent experiments, showing similar difficulty scaling in a different action space.
Cost analysis is transparent and grounded in disclosed token pricing and computation, and reproducibility support (full prompts, action space statistics, code/data release commitment) is good.
The base-generator ablation (Table 6) addresses the natural concern that the results are an artifact of GPT-4.1 as the synthesis model.
weaknesses: The benchmark's ground truth rests on an LLM verifier with only 88% agreement with humans and a 12% false-accept rate on near-miss perturbations. For a benchmark whose headline result is very low success rates, even a few-percent verifier error is a substantial fraction of the measured signal, and error bars on model comparisons are not provided.

Evaluation sample sizes are small: 50 tasks per difficulty level for model evaluation and only 20 tasks for the human comparison. Differences like 4% vs. 0% between frontier models are within statistical noise at this scale, yet the paper draws conclusions about relative model performance and benchmark discrimination.

The claimed utility of the 6,000 tasks/trajectories for training is not demonstrated—there is no downstream fine-tuning experiment showing that AgentSynth trajectories improve agent performance, which weakens the 'unlocking significant potential for agent training' framing.

The trajectory generator (GPT-4.1 planner + computer-use-preview) is also one of the evaluated models, creating a potential circularity that, while partially addressed by the generator ablation, is not fully discussed.

Novelty is incremental in places: the pipeline composes known components (persona hub, OSWorld, WebJudge-style verification, ReAct execution), and chaining atomic tasks to increase difficulty has precedent in WorkArena++/Boisvert et al.; the information-asymmetry framing, while elegant, is close to Li et al. (2025).

Several presentation issues undermine polish: the URL in the abstract is missing, 'the top panel of Figure 4' refers to a grouped bar chart with no panels, the prompt templates contain numerous typos ('clike', 'controll'), and rule numbering skips values—raising concerns about attention to detail.
Human performance is evaluated only on 20 level-6 tasks, making the '70% human success' claim—and hence the size of the human-machine gap—statistically fragile.
Contamination and staleness risks from tasks requiring live web content (e.g., searching for specific statistics) are not addressed; task verifiability may degrade over time.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting information asymmetry—composing verified, easy-to-generate subtasks into long-horizon tasks—is intuitive and well-motivated, and the ablation in Table 5 cleanly demonstrates the decoupling of generation success from evaluation difficulty.

The paper is thorough about validating the pipeline: human evaluation of task quality (Table 1), verifier calibration against human judgments (Figure 2), and an adversarial near-miss stress test of the verifier (Table 2) are all commendable practices that many synthetic-data papers omit.
Cost analysis (Table 3, Appendix E) is transparent about assumptions and makes the scalability claim concrete and reproducible.

The ablations on scaffolding (Agent S3/S2.5) and on the base generator model (Table 6) show the qualitative conclusions are not an artifact of one particular backbone, which strengthens the benchmarking claims.
Prompt templates, action space statistics, and an anonymized code release support reasonably good reproducibility of the pipeline itself.
weaknesses: Circularity in evaluation: the same LLM-based verifier is used both to construct the dataset (deciding task success and revising tasks) and to score agents on the benchmark. With verifier accuracy of only 88% against humans (Table 1), the label noise (~12%) is three times larger than the headline success rates at hard levels (e.g., 4% with 50 tasks per level ≈ 2 successes), so the steep decline in Figure 4 and the 'near-zero success' claims are not statistically distinguishable from verification noise. No confidence intervals or human re-verification of agent failures on hard levels are provided.

No demonstration of training utility: the paper's central selling point is a scalable trajectory dataset for training generalist agents, yet there are zero fine-tuning or SFT/RL experiments. The entire value proposition of 6,000 trajectories rests on unvalidated assumptions about their quality as training data, especially given that trajectories come from a planner+grounding pair (GPT-4.1 + computer-use-preview) whose traces may be inconsistent or low-diversity.

Task verifiability and reproducibility are weak: many generated tasks depend on live, changing web content (e.g., 'search for recidivism rate statistics,' 'find the 2024 commencement date'), which makes ground truth non-deterministic and the benchmark non-stationary. Success on such tasks partially measures whether the model hallucinates plausible-looking data that the screenshot-based verifier accepts—an issue the adversarial test does not address for open-ended retrieval tasks.

Limited novelty: chaining atomic tasks into compositional tasks is closely related to WorkArena++ (Boisvert et al., 2024), which the paper acknowledges; the 'information asymmetry' framing is borrowed from Li et al. (2025). The main novelty is applying this to the OSWorld environment, which is incremental.

Task diversity appears overstated: the examples in Appendix D show highly templated, near-duplicate task families (the same 'experiment1.py' and 'anonymous tip' scaffolds repeated across difficulty levels), suggesting the '6,000 diverse tasks' may have substantially lower effective diversity than claimed, which is precisely the model-collapse risk the introduction warns about.

Evaluation of 'state-of-the-art agents' uses bare LLMs with a single pyautogui prompt (a known-weak setup), and while scaffolding experiments are added, the overall suite is thin: only ~50 tasks per level, no comparison to published OSWorld numbers or standardized agent harnesses, making cross-benchmark comparability difficult.

Human evaluation is small (100 instances, ~16 per difficulty level) with limited detail on annotator guidelines, screening, or disagreement resolution beyond one kappa value; conclusions about 90%+ quality rates are therefore fragile.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'precisely modulate task complexity' is asserted, but difficulty levels conflate horizon length with web-content dependence and task ambiguity (visible in the level 4–6 task descriptions in Appendix D, which become verbose and partially redundant rather than cleanly harder).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: the lack of scalable, diverse task/trajectory data for generalist computer-use agents, and clearly motivates why existing human-annotated datasets (OSWorld, TheAgentCompany, tau-bench) are too costly to scale.

The core idea of information asymmetry — chaining simple, verifiable subtasks forward and only afterwards summarizing them into long-horizon tasks — is simple, well-articulated, and demonstrably effective: Table 5 shows the pipeline achieves high generation success (52-65%) even at hard difficulty, where the direct-instruction baseline collapses (11% at Hard), while evaluation difficulty remains high (14% at level 6).

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a dataset/benchmark paper: human quality assessment with inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.74), verifier calibration against human judgments across difficulty levels, an adversarial stress test of the verifier (near-miss vs. benign perturbations), cost analysis with transparent assumptions (Appendix E), multi-scaffold evaluation (bare LLMs, Agent S2.5, Agent S3), a generator-model ablation (Table 6), and a transfer of the pipeline to a second environment (InSTA) demonstrating generality.

The benchmark is discriminative and well-positioned against related work: clear performance degradation with difficulty (18% to 4%), near-zero performance at high levels, human baseline (70% on level 6), and a comparison table (Table 4) that fairly situates AgentSynth against existing benchmarks.

Reproducibility is supported by complete prompt templates (Appendices B, F), action space documentation (Appendix G), cost accounting, and stated intent to release code and data; the ethics statement addresses safety concerns about autonomous web interaction.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between the verifier used in generation and evaluation: the same LLM-based verifier (WebJudge-style) both certifies ground-truth trajectories during data synthesis and scores agent success at benchmark time. Although human calibration (88% agreement) and the adversarial stress test mitigate this, a 12% false-positive rate on near-miss failures directly inflates reported agent success rates on a benchmark where models score 4-18%; error bars on this inflation are not quantified.

The paper claims the dataset is valuable for 'training and evaluating' agents, but provides no downstream training experiment showing that fine-tuning on AgentSynth trajectories actually improves agent performance. The training utility claim is thus unsupported, which is a significant limitation for a 6,000-task trajectory dataset.

The evaluation sets are small (50 tasks per difficulty level; 20 for the human baseline), so per-level success rates (e.g., 0.02 vs 0.04) rest on one or two tasks, and no statistical significance testing is provided despite error bars in only some figures.

Because tasks depend on live websites and dynamic web content, trajectory validity and benchmark reproducibility over time are questionable (link rot, changing pages), and this threat to long-term benchmark utility is not discussed.

Tasks are generated and executed by GPT-4.1-based agents with a maximum of 10 steps per subtask and verification-based revision, which may bias the distribution toward tasks the generator model can already solve, potentially limiting diversity in ways not fully characterized; the sample of 100 instances for human evaluation (~16 per level) is small for the diversity claims.

Some difficulty 'levels' largely reflect the length of a natural-language summary of the same subtask chain (Appendix D), so the measured difficulty axis conflates horizon length with instruction ambiguity — longer descriptions may be easier to follow in some respects, complicating interpretation of the difficulty trend.
